title: Dysphagia screening and nutrition after stroke
blurb: Keep people safe from aspiration after stroke: screen before anything by mouth, escalate to specialists, and start tube feeding and medicine changes on time.
question: Mr Kowalski, 72, arrives on the stroke unit with a left hemiparesis and slurred speech. He asks for a cup of tea and his evening tablets. No swallow screen has been done yet. What should the nurse do?

teach.body: Dysphagia is difficulty moving food, fluid or saliva safely from mouth to stomach. After a stroke it is common, and it can be silent: food or fluid enters the airway without coughing. Aspiration leads to pneumonia, dehydration and malnutrition. Plain English: until a trained person has checked the swallow, nothing goes in by mouth, including tablets and sips of water.

steps.label: Nil by mouth
steps.sub: No food, fluid or medicine yet

steps.label: Specialist review
steps.sub: Preferably within 24 h, at most 72 h

steps.label: Plan
steps.sub: Diet, fluids, medicines, or tube feeding

teach.caption: The National Clinical Guideline for Stroke (2023) also sets a screen within 4 hours of arrival.

teach.caption: The 24-hour NG feeding rule has one stated exception: people who have had thrombolysis.

teach.body: If the person cannot take adequate nutrition, fluids and medicines orally, NICE says they should have nasogastric tube feeding within 24 hours of admission (unless they have had thrombolysis). Consider a nasal bridle or gastrostomy if the NG tube is not tolerated. Refer to a trained professional (usually a dietitian) for nutritional assessment, and review every oral medicine so its formulation or route can be changed.

children.label: Oral intake as advised
children.sub: Watch for coughing, wet voice, fatigue

children.label: Stay nil by mouth
children.sub: Specialist assessment, NG feeding within 24 h, medicine review

teach.caption: Suspected aspiration, or tube feeding or modified diet for 3 days: reassess, consider instrumental examination, refer for dietary advice (NG128 1.6.3).

teach.text: Medicines are oral intake too. A failed screen means no tablets by mouth, even 'just with a sip'. Do not crush tablets on your own initiative: ask the prescriber and pharmacist to change the formulation or route. Aspirin 300 mg goes rectally or by enteral tube.

teach.h: Scenario: Mrs Abiola on the stroke unit
teach.body: Mrs Abiola, 77, had an ischaemic stroke and was not thrombolysed. At 14:00 she fails her admission swallow screen. The nurse keeps her nil by mouth, refers her to speech and language therapy, gives her aspirin 300 mg rectally as prescribed, and asks for her oral medicines to be reviewed. By the next morning she still cannot take enough orally, so an NG tube is placed within 24 hours of admission and its position is confirmed by pH before use.

teach.caption: Routine supplements are not recommended for people with stroke who are adequately nourished on admission (NG128 1.6.9).

items: Screen the swallow before any oral food, fluid or medicine.
Failed screen: specialist assessment preferably within 24 hours, no later than 72 hours.
Can't take enough orally: NG feeding within 24 hours of admission (unless thrombolysed).
NG not tolerated: consider nasal bridle or gastrostomy; refer for dietetic assessment.
Review every oral medicine; aspirin 300 mg rectally or by enteral tube.

summary: You can now keep a person with acute stroke nil by mouth until a trained screen, escalate a failed screen for specialist assessment within NICE time limits, and start NG feeding on time. You can also make sure their medicines and nutrition are reviewed so nothing is given unsafely by mouth.

A.q: Mrs Grant, 81, has just arrived on the stroke unit with right-sided weakness. Her daughter offers her a drink of water. No swallow screen has been completed. What should the nurse do?
options: Offer thickened water from a teaspoon
Let her sip water while sitting fully upright
Keep her nil by mouth until she is screened
Offer water if she can cough on request
A.why: NICE NG128 rec 1.6.1: people with acute stroke must have their swallow screened by a trained professional before any oral food, fluid or medicine.

whyNot.0: Thickened fluid is still oral intake and needs a screen and specialist advice first.
whyNot.1: Upright positioning does not make an unscreened swallow safe; aspiration can be silent.
whyNot.3: A voluntary cough does not test the swallow and is not a screen.

A.q: Mr Ito fails his admission swallow screen. Within what time should he preferably have a specialist assessment of swallowing?
A.why: NICE NG128 rec 1.6.2: specialist assessment of swallowing preferably within 24 hours of admission and not more than 72 hours afterwards.

whyNot.0: 4 hours is the national guideline target for the initial screen, not for the specialist assessment.
whyNot.2: 7 days is far beyond the 72-hour maximum.
whyNot.3: NICE times this from admission, preferably within 24 hours; 48 hours from the screen is not the standard.

A.q: Mrs Fernandes, 70, had an ischaemic stroke but was not thrombolysed. She cannot take adequate nutrition, fluid or medicines orally. When should nasogastric tube feeding start?
options: Once she has lost 5% of her weight
A.why: NICE NG128 rec 1.6.4: people with acute stroke unable to take adequate nutrition, fluids and medicines orally should receive NG tube feeding within 24 hours of admission (unless they have had thrombolysis).

whyNot.1: 72 hours is the outer limit for specialist swallow assessment, not for starting feeding.
whyNot.2: Waiting for weight loss allows avoidable malnutrition.
whyNot.3: She cannot swallow safely, so oral supplements are not an option.

B.q: Mr Harris has failed his swallow screen and is prescribed his usual oral atorvastatin, amlodipine and aspirin 300 mg. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Crush the tablets and give them in yoghurt
Give them with a teaspoon of thickened water
Omit them until the SLT has seen him
Ask for review of route and formulation
B.why: NICE NG128 rec 1.6.4: people unable to take medicines orally should have their oral medication reviewed to amend the formulation or route. Aspirin can be given rectally or by enteral tube (1.4.9).

whyNot.0: Crushed tablets in yoghurt are still oral, and altering a medicine's form needs pharmacist and prescriber advice.
whyNot.1: Any oral route is unsafe after a failed screen.
whyNot.2: Simply omitting them risks missing aspirin and other needed medicines; a route review is needed now.

B.q: Mrs Kaur cannot tolerate her nasogastric tube and has pulled it out twice. She still cannot swallow safely. What should be considered next?
options: A nasal bridle tube or gastrostomy
B.why: NICE NG128 rec 1.6.4: consider a nasal bridle tube or gastrostomy if the person cannot tolerate a nasogastric tube.

whyNot.1: She cannot swallow safely, so supervised oral supplements still risk aspiration.
whyNot.2: Peripheral IV fluids hydrate but do not provide nutrition.
whyNot.3: A normal diet is unsafe until a specialist assessment says otherwise.

B.q: A newly placed nasogastric tube needs checking before the first feed. Which result confirms gastric placement?
B.why: NICE CG32 (core facts): check NG tube position after placement and before each use; aspirate pH 5.5 or below on pH paper supports gastric placement, with X-ray if needed.

whyNot.0: pH 6.5 is above 5.5 and does not confirm gastric placement.
whyNot.1: Auscultation ('whoosh' test) is unreliable and must not be used.
whyNot.3: Litmus paper is not a safe test of NG position.

C.q: Mr Adeyemi, 64, had thrombolysis for an ischaemic stroke 6 hours ago and has failed his swallow screen. The registrar asks about feeding. Which statement best reflects NICE NG128?
options: He needs an NG tube within 2 hours
Thrombolysis is the exception to the 24-hour rule
He needs a gastrostomy within 24 hours
He may have oral supplements as he was thrombolysed
C.why: NICE NG128 rec 1.6.4: NG feeding within 24 hours of admission applies unless the person has had thrombolysis. He still needs specialist swallow assessment, nutrition review and medicine review.

whyNot.0: There is no 2-hour NG target; and thrombolysis is the named exception.
whyNot.2: Gastrostomy is considered if an NG tube is not tolerated, not as a 24-hour target.
whyNot.3: Thrombolysis does not make an unsafe swallow safe; oral intake still needs specialist advice.

C.q: Mrs Moreau has needed a modified-texture diet for 3 days after her stroke, and the SLT suspects she is aspirating. Which plan follows NICE guidance?
options: Continue the same diet and review her at discharge
Change her to a normal diet and observe closely
Start NG feeding and discharge her from SLT input
Reassess, consider instrumental tests, dietetic referral
C.why: NICE NG128 rec 1.6.3: people with suspected aspiration, or who need tube feeding or dietary modification for 3 days, should be reassessed and considered for instrumental examination, and referred for dietary advice.

whyNot.0: Waiting until discharge ignores suspected aspiration and the 3-day reassessment trigger.
whyNot.1: A normal diet increases aspiration risk when aspiration is suspected.
whyNot.2: Feeding may be needed, but SLT reassessment continues; it is not stopped.

C.q: Mr Lewis, 69, passed his swallow screen and is eating well 2 days after a stroke. His MUST score on admission was 0. A relative asks whether he should have nutritional supplement drinks. What is the best response?
options: Yes, everyone gets them for the first week
Yes, until his speech has recovered
C.why: NICE NG128 recs 1.6.5 and 1.6.9: routine nutritional supplementation is not recommended for people with acute stroke who are adequately nourished on admission; repeat malnutrition screening weekly.

whyNot.0: NICE does not recommend routine supplements for adequately nourished people.
whyNot.1: Supplements are started for malnutrition risk, which he does not currently have.
whyNot.3: Speech recovery is not an indication for supplements; nutritional risk is.

reteach.title: The locked front door
reteach.question: Think of the mouth as a front door that stays locked until someone with the key has checked it. Who holds the key, and what happens if the door won't open?

blocks.h: Lock, check, then choose another door
blocks.body: The door is locked on arrival: nothing by mouth, not even tablets. A trained professional screens the swallow. If the door won't open safely, a speech and language therapist assesses within 24 hours (72 at most). Meanwhile, nutrition and medicines use another door: an NG tube within 24 hours of admission (unless thrombolysed), rectal aspirin, and a review of every oral medicine.

blocks.text: Thickened fluids, yoghurt and 'just a sip' are all oral intake. None is safe before a screen.

explain.body: On admission, a trained healthcare professional screens the swallow before any oral food, fluid or medication. The national stroke guideline sets this within 4 hours of arrival.

test.q: Who should carry out the admission swallow screen after an acute stroke?
options: Any member of staff on duty
The consultant on the post-take round
test.why: NICE NG128 rec 1.6.1: an appropriately trained healthcare professional screens the swallow.

whyNot.0: Untrained staff should not screen swallowing.
whyNot.1: Relatives are not trained to screen and should be told to wait.
whyNot.3: Waiting for the post-take round delays the screen; any trained professional can do it.

explain.body: If the screen shows problems, the person needs specialist assessment, preferably within 24 hours of admission and no later than 72 hours. Suspected aspiration, or 3 days of tube feeding or modified diet, triggers reassessment and dietary referral.

test.q: What is the latest time NICE accepts for a specialist swallow assessment after a failed screen?
test.why: NICE NG128 rec 1.6.2: preferably within 24 hours of admission and not more than 72 hours afterwards.

whyNot.1: 24 hours is the preferred target, not the latest limit.
whyNot.3: Discharge may be weeks away; the limit is 72 hours.

explain.body: Unable to take adequate nutrition, fluids and medicines orally: NG feeding within 24 hours of admission unless they had thrombolysis; bridle or gastrostomy if NG not tolerated; dietetic assessment.

test.q: Which professional should provide detailed nutritional assessment and individualised advice for a person with stroke who needs tube feeding?
test.why: NICE NG128 rec 1.6.4: refer to an appropriately trained healthcare professional for detailed nutritional assessment, individualised advice and monitoring; NG128 1.6.3 also specifies referral for dietary advice. In practice this is a dietitian.

whyNot.0: OTs support function and feeding aids, not nutritional prescription.
whyNot.2: The pharmacist reviews medicine formulations, not nutritional requirements.
whyNot.3: Physiotherapists lead mobility and chest care, not nutrition.

explain.body: Oral medicines are reviewed so the formulation or route can be changed. Aspirin 300 mg goes rectally or by enteral tube in dysphagia. Do not crush tablets without pharmacist and prescriber advice.

test.q: A person with acute ischaemic stroke and dysphagia is prescribed aspirin 300 mg. Which route is appropriate?
test.why: NICE NG128 rec 1.4.9: aspirin 300 mg rectally or by enteral tube if the person has dysphagia.

whyNot.0: Sublingual aspirin is not the NG128 route and still relies on the mouth.
whyNot.3: Thickened oral intake is still oral and unsafe without assessment.
